title: Numbers to know
objectives: Estimate √2, e, ln 2, π² and powers of 2 to two figures, and use the rule of 72.

screens.title: From £1 to a million
screens.prose: Start with £1 and double it again and again. The line is on a log scale, so each doubling is one equal step. Slide the doublings.
screens.question: How many doublings take £1 past £1 million?

hints.text: Slide until the blue dot passes the orange one.
19 doublings give £524,288; one more doubles it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the first power of 2 above a million.

byKey.six: A million is $10^6$, but each step only doubles. You need far more than six.

explain.text: 19 doublings give £524,288 and 20 give £1,048,576. So 20 doublings pass £1 million. Principle: ten doublings are about a thousandfold.

screens.title: Ten doublings, a thousandfold

state.caption: Each power of 2 sits just right of its power of 10.

screens.question: What is $2^{32}$ in billions, to two decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $2^{30} = 1.074$ billion, then multiply by 4.

byKey.rough: 4 uses $2^{30} = 10^9$. The 2.4% excess compounds to 7.4% by $2^{30}$.
byKey.one: That is $2^{31}$. $2^{32}$ is twice as big.

explain.text: $2^{30} = 1.074 \times 10^9$ and $2^{32} = 4 \times 2^{30}$. So $2^{32} = 4.29$ billion, the count of 32-bit values. Principle: carry the small excess when you scale $2^{10} \approx 10^3$.

screens.title: Square root of 2 by bracketing
screens.prose: In mental l8-squaring you squared numbers quickly; here that skill traps a root. Drag $x$ and watch $x^2$ cross 2. The lesson mental-pressure l8 drills roots at speed.
screens.question: What is $\sqrt{2}$ to two decimal places?

widget.label: Root
widget.accept: 1.41, or a closer rounding such as 1.414 or 1.4142

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bracket 2 between two squares, then test the midpoint.

byKey.up: $1.42^2 = 2.0164$ overshoots, and $1.415^2 = 2.002$ does too. So the root is below 1.415.
byKey.one: $1.40^2 = 1.96$ is too small. Try one more hundredth.

explain.text: $1.41^2 = 1.9881$ and $1.42^2 = 2.0164$ bracket 2. The midpoint $1.415^2 = 2.0022$ is above 2, so the root rounds down to 1.41. Principle: bracket, then test the midpoint before rounding.

screens.title: Why 72
screens.prose: Money at $r$% a year doubles in $T = \ln 2 / \ln(1 + r/100)$ years. The curve shows the number $rT$ that a rule should use. Drag P along it.

derive.caption: At {{fixed(P.x, 1)}}%: exact time {{fixed(ln(2) / ln(1 + P.x / 100), 2)}} years; 72/r gives {{fixed(72 / P.x, 2)}}.

screens.question: At 8%, which rule is closer to the exact doubling time?

options.why: 69.3 is right only as the rate falls to 0. At 8% it gives 8.66 years, 0.34 short of 9.006.

hints.text: Drag P to 8% and read the curve.

feedback.correct: 72: at 8% the exact time is 9.006 years.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each rule with the curve at 8%.

byKey.69: The curve starts near 69.3 at low rates and rises. At 8% it is 72.05.
byKey.same: At 8% the curve sits on 72, well above 69.3.

explain.text: At 8% the exact time is 9.006 years and $72/8 = 9$. At 6% it is 11.90 against 12. Principle: the right numerator rises with the rate, and 72 fits ordinary rates.

screens.title: Any rate at all
screens.prose: A colleague says the rule of 72 works at any rate. At 36% it says 2 years. Use $\ln 2 = 0.6931$ and $\ln 1.36 = 0.3075$.
screens.question: What is the exact doubling time at 36%, in years? Give two decimal places.

feedback.correct: 2.25 years, a quarter more than the rule says.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the exact formula, not the rule.

byKey.rule: 2 is the rule's answer. At 36% the right numerator is 81, so the exact time is 2.25.
byKey.small: $69.3/36 = 1.93$ is further off still. Divide the logs.

explain.text: $0.6931 / 0.3075 = 2.254$ years against the rule's 2. At 36% the right numerator is 81, not 72. Principle: a rule built for small rates breaks at large ones.

screens.title: A short table to carry
screens.prose:
Every answer came from a few numbers and how they combine.

| | | | |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| $\sqrt{2}$ | 1.414 | $\ln 2$ | 0.693 |
| $\sqrt{3}$ | 1.732 | $\ln 10$ | 2.303 |
| $e$ | 2.718 | $\pi^2$ | 9.870 |
| $1/e$ | 0.368 | $2^{10}$ | 1,024 |

Doubling takes $\tfrac{\ln 2}{\ln(1 + r)} \approx \tfrac{69.3}{r}$ years. 72 corrects for ordinary rates and divides easily.
screens.question: Build $\ln 5$ from the table, to two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A quotient becomes a difference of logs.

byKey.sum: You added the logs, which gives $\ln 20$. Five is ten divided by two.
byKey.ratio: You divided the logs. $\ln(10/2)$ is a difference, not a quotient.

explain.text: $5 = 10/2$, so $\ln 5 = 2.303 - 0.693 = 1.610$. Principle: logs turn products and quotients into sums and differences.

screens.title: Where 69.3 comes from
screens.prose: Derive the doubling time at a small yearly rate $r$. Two lines may swap, and one does not belong.
screens.question: Order the derivation.

lines.why: That is simple interest: it ignores compounding and gives 12.5 years at 8%.

hints.text: Logs bring $T$ down from the power.

feedback.correct: Doubling, logs, the small-rate step, then the rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take logs before you approximate.

byKey.d1: $1 + rT$ drops the interest on interest. Take logs instead.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the simple-interest line belongs.

explain.text: Logs give $T = \ln 2 / \ln(1 + r)$ exactly, and $\ln(1 + r) \approx r$ gives $69.3/r$. The next term, $-r^2/2$, makes $\ln(1 + r)$ smaller, so the true numerator is bigger. Principle: 72 absorbs that correction near 8%.

screens.title: Drill: pi squared
screens.prose: Drill, about a minute each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Give $\pi^2$ to two decimal places.
screens.question: What is $\pi^2$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square $3.1416$ by parts.

byKey.twice: That is $2\pi$. Squaring multiplies π by itself.

explain.text: $(3 + 0.1416)^2 = 9 + 0.8496 + 0.0201 = 9.8696$. So $\pi^2 = 9.87$, just under 10. Principle: square a number by splitting off its whole part.

screens.title: Drill: doubling at 9%
screens.prose: Drill, about a minute each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Money grows at 9% a year, compounded yearly.
screens.question: About how many years does it take to double? Give two figures.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 72 by the rate.

byKey.ln2: $69.3/9 = 7.7$ is the small-rate rule. At 9% the numerator is about 72.
byKey.simple: $100/9$ is simple interest. Compounding is faster.

explain.text: $72/9 = 8$, and the exact $\ln 2 / \ln 1.09 = 8.04$. Principle: near 8% the rule of 72 is good to a few hundredths.

screens.title: Drill: one per cent, a hundred times
screens.prose: Drill, about a minute each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Work out $1.01^{100}$ to two decimal places. Compare it with $e$.
screens.question: What is $1.01^{100}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $1.01^{100}$ is a little below $e$.

byKey.e: $e$ is the limit of $(1 + 1/n)^n$. At $n = 100$ the value is still below it: 2.705.
byKey.simple: 2 is simple interest. Compounding adds interest on interest.

explain.text: $100 \ln 1.01 = 0.995$, so $1.01^{100} = e^{0.995} = 2.705$. That is $e$ less half a per cent. Principle: $(1 + x)^n \approx e^{nx}$ for small $x$.

screens.title: Four times the money
screens.prose: Follow-up. The interviewer asks how long £1 takes to quadruple at 8% a year. A desk uses this to sanity-check a fund's projected growth in seconds.
screens.question: About how many years does £1 take to become £4 at 8%?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the doublings in a factor of 4.

byKey.four: Quadrupling is two doublings, not four.

explain.text: A factor of 4 is two doublings of 9 years each, so 18 years. Exactly, $\ln 4 / \ln 1.08 = 18.01$. Principle: convert any growth factor into doublings.

screens.title: Ten times the money
screens.prose: Follow-up. Now the interviewer asks for a tenfold rise at 8%. Ten is not a whole number of doublings: $\log_2 10 = 3.32$.
screens.question: About how many years does £1 take to become £10 at 8%?

hints.text: Count the doublings in a factor of 10.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply 3.32 doublings by 9 years.

explain.text: Tenfold is $\log_2 10 = 3.32$ doublings, and $3.32 \times 9 = 29.9$ years. Exactly, $\ln 10 / \ln 1.08 = 29.92$. Principle: $\ln 10 / \ln 2 = 3.32$ turns powers of 10 into doublings.

ideas: Carry a short table: √2, √3, e, ln 2, ln 10, π², 1/e and 2¹⁰ ≈ 10³.
Build other values from it: logs turn products into sums, and powers of 2 scale by thousands.
Doubling takes ln 2 / ln(1 + r) years, about 72/r at ordinary rates.

formula.name: Doubling time
formula.note: Good near 8%; at 36% the exact time is 2.25, not 2.

summary.trap: The rule of 72 is built for ordinary rates: at 36% it says 2 years, and the truth is 2.25.

quiz.prose: Compare $e^{\pi}$ and $\pi^{e}$ without a calculator. Take logs of both.
quiz.question: Which is larger?

options.why: You let the larger base win. Compare logs: $\pi = 3.142$ against $e \ln \pi = 3.112$.
Their logs are 3.142 and 3.112, which differ.

byKey.pie: A bigger base does not settle it. The logs are $\pi = 3.1416$ and $e \ln \pi = 3.1117$.
byKey.eq: The logs differ by 0.03, so the numbers differ.

explain.text: $\ln e^{\pi} = \pi = 3.1416$ and $\ln \pi^{e} = e \ln \pi = 2.718 \times 1.1447 = 3.1117$. So $e^{\pi}$ is larger: 23.14 against 22.46. Principle: compare powers by their logs.

quiz.prose: The rule of 72 says money at 72% a year doubles in 1 year. Use $\ln 1.72 = 0.5423$.
quiz.question: What is the exact doubling time, in years? Give two decimal places.

byKey.rule: 1 is the rule's answer. At 72% the rule is off by more than a quarter.

explain.text: $0.6931 / 0.5423 = 1.278$ years against the rule's 1. At large rates the rule is badly short. Principle: check a rule at the edge of its range.

quiz.prose: Work out $0.99^{100}$ to three decimal places. Compare it with $1/e = 0.368$.
quiz.question: What is $0.99^{100}$?

byKey.inv: $1/e$ is the limit. At $n = 100$ the value is a little lower: 0.366.
byKey.simple: Losing 1% a hundred times is not losing 100%. Each loss is 1% of what is left.

quiz.question: What is $\ln 2$ to two decimal places?

byKey.e: 0.72 is the rule-of-72 numerator over 100, not $\ln 2$.

explain.text: $\ln 2 \approx 0.3 \times 2.303 = 0.691$, close to the true 0.6931. Principle: $2^{10} \approx 10^3$ links base 2 to base 10.

byKey.double: 512 is $2^9$. Doubling the power squares the number.
byKey.approx: 64,000 uses $2^{10} = 1000$. The question asks for the exact value.

explain.text: $2^{16} = 256^2 = 65{,}536$, the number of 16-bit values. Principle: square to double the power.
